transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Lindqvist, I need to talk to you about the blood transfusion you received during your surgery yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is there a problem? I've been feeling a bit off since I woke up.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry, but there was a mistake in our process. The team didn't perform the pre-operative blood type verification before the transfusion.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do you mean by that? You didn't cross-match?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We didn't follow the verification protocol, so you received a compatible unit, but it wasn't the ideal match for your specific blood type.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, you're telling me you just guessed? Or you just took a gamble with my life because you couldn't be bothered to check a label?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, it wasn't a guess, it was a failure in our checklist process. I am very sorry that this happened. Our team is responsible for this error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I spent fifteen years as a paramedic. I know exactly how catastrophic a transfusion reaction can be. Do you have any idea how terrified I am right now? I can feel my heart racing and I don't know if I'm having a reaction or if I'm just losing my mind.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see that you're feeling scared and angry right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Scared? I'm beyond scared. I'm wondering if I'm going to go into renal failure because some resident forgot how to read a chart. How does this even happen in a modern hospital?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It shouldn't have happened. We had a breakdown in the verification step—

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't want to hear about breakdowns! I want to know if I'm dying. Am I in danger? Give me a straight answer.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have to go check on another patient in a moment, but let's look at the facts. Because the blood was compatible, the risk of a severe hemolytic reaction is low.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Low isn't zero. You just admitted to a gross negligence of protocol.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand this is incredibly frustrating.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frustrating? This is an assault on my safety. I trusted you people. Who is the attending? I want the attending in here right now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can certainly arrange for the attending to come by later.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Later? I want them here now. I can't stop shaking. I keep thinking about the possibilities of what's happening in my veins right now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: But if we just look at the monitors—

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care about the monitors! I care that you skipped a basic safety step! How could you possibly—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Let's just quickly wrap this up so we can get a plan in place.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Don't you dare tell me to wrap this up. You've just told me you messed up my blood and now you're rushing out the door?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry, I just mean we need to move toward the solution.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The solution is telling me exactly what you are doing to monitor me. Now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are going to keep an eye on your vitals and we'll probably run some more labs tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Tomorrow? That's your plan? A "probably" tomorrow?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll make sure the nursing staff checks your urine output for any signs of hemoglobinuria today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then what? What happens if the labs come back abnormal?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will address that if it happens.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is unbelievable. You've stripped away every bit of trust I had in this surgical team.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize you're very upset.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am beyond upset. I am documenting every single word of this. This is a sentinel event.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Who is auditing this? Is there a formal incident report?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There will be a review.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I want a copy of that report. I want to know who skipped the verification and why.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can't promise a copy of the internal review, but I can tell you that we are reporting it to the board.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't even breathe properly. I feel like I'm suffocating.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I think you're just having an anxiety response to the news.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Or I'm having a delayed transfusion reaction! Did that even cross your mind?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Your vitals are currently stable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Stable is not the same as safe!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I truly am sorry that this happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Your apology doesn't change the blood in my system.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When is the attending coming?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll send them a page and they should be here sometime this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Get out. Just get out and go find your boss.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('I have to go check on another patient', 'quickly wrap this up') and interrupts the patient's emotional distress.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly in the second turn, but there were no comprehension checks performed throughout the conversation.

A.justification: Resident used direct apology language, explicitly stated 'Our team is responsible for this error', and maintained this accountability under pushback.

R.justification: Resident named specific emotions ('scared and angry') and attempted to engage, though later responses became more factual.

T.justification: Resident provided vague steps (checking urine today, labs 'probably' tomorrow) with no named patient role and no discussion of prevention.
